english.html: quished — it comes about that the seed which afterwards flows forth, having nothing but of the body (for the mind was wandering elsewhere), has likewise not much reasonable and natural virtue <sup class="mk" data-key="n">n</sup>: which was (in the judgment of many) the cause why Aristarchus of Alexandria, a man of singular and commendable erudition, nevertheless begot Aristagoras and Aristarchus, his children, dull, stolid and almost simpletons <sup class="mk" data-key="o">o</sup>. On this subject the reader will take it in good part if I transcribe the words of Spartianus, who, writing to the Emperor Diocletian: It is certain (said he), Augustus, that there has been almost none of those great and illustrious personages who have left children good and useful to the commonwealth: for either they died without having any, or else had such that it would have been better for them beyond comparison never to have had any. And to begin with Romulus: he had no posterity. Numa Pompilius, his successor, had none who could profit the public. And then Camillus: had he children like himself? And Scipio, what? The Catos, what? — who were excellent and rare persons. But what shall I say of Homer, Demosthenes, Virgil, Sallust, Plautus, Terence? And what, moreover, of Caesar? And what of Cicero, for whom alone it would have been better to have had no children? What of Augustus, who did not even have a good adopted son, although he had the power to choose a good one out of a hundred thousand? Was not Trajan deceived in the choice he made of Hadrian his nephew? But let us come to natural sons. What greater good fortune could have come to Marcus Antoninus, Philosopher and Emperor, than if he had not left Commodus his heir? and to Septimius Severus, if he had not begotten Bassianus <sup class="mk" data-key="p">p</sup>? But to return to our track, and to search curiously into the cause of likenesses: I do not find amiss the opinion of Empedocles and of the natural philosophers, who think that this proceeds from the imagination which the woman may have conceived at the hour when she conceives, which has such power over the fruit that comes to be formed that the character of the image remains perpetually engraved upon it <sup class="mk" data-key="q">q</sup>. notes.citation: Accursius, gloss on Digest 50.16 (De verborum significatione), l. Quaeret aliquis (cf. D. 50.16.135, Ulpian, on monstrous births), and on Digest 1.5 (De statu hominum), l. Non sunt liberi (cf. D. 1.5.14, Paulus)

notes.gloss: Both fragments concern children born "against the form of the human race"; the gloss carries the doctrine of the mother's imagination.
